tool.name: spaCy
tool.tagline: Industrial-strength NLP pipelines for tokenizing, tagging, parsing and entities
tool.description: spaCy is a fast, production-oriented NLP library. A trained pipeline turns text into a Doc with tokens, lemmas, part-of-speech tags, dependency parses, sentences and named entities, and you can add rule-based matchers, custom components or transformer models. It is a common choice for information extraction and text processing services.

glossary.def: Getting computers to work with human language: splitting text into words, finding names, working out sentence structure, judging tone and so on.
In spaCy, the series of processing steps that run in order on your text, such as splitting it into tokens, tagging words and finding names. A trained pipeline comes as its own installable package.
One processing step in a spaCy pipeline, such as the tagger, the parser or the ner step. Each takes a Doc, adds information to it and passes it on.
One piece of text after it has been split up: usually a word, a number or a punctuation mark.
spaCy's object for a processed text: the sequence of tokens plus everything the pipeline worked out about them. You get one from nlp(text).
A slice of a Doc covering one or more neighbouring tokens. Sentences, entities and matches are all spans.
A list of numbers describing a word, learned so that words used in similar ways get similar numbers. Used to measure how alike words or texts are.
The dictionary form of a word, the one you would look up: 'run' for 'running', 'mouse' for 'mice'.
A label saying what kind of word a token is in its sentence: noun, verb, adjective and so on. spaCy writes them as codes like NOUN and VERB.
A very common word such as 'the', 'of' or 'and' that says little about what a text is about, and is often skipped.
A map of how the words of a sentence connect: each word points to the word it depends on (its head), with a label such as 'subject of' or 'object of'.
A noun together with the words that describe it, such as 'the striped bats' or 'ripe mangoes'.
Finding names of real-world things in text and saying what kind they are: a person, a company, a place, a date, an amount of money and so on.
A way to mark entities one tag per token: B for the first token of an entity, I for a token inside one, and O for a token outside any entity.
An attribute you add yourself to spaCy's Doc, Token or Span objects, read under ._ such as doc._.urgent.

A kind of large neural network that reads a whole passage at once and weighs how every word relates to every other. It is the design behind modern AI language models and spaCy's most accurate pipelines.
spaCy's pipeline component that turns each token into a list of numbers that later components, such as the tagger and parser, use.
In a spaCy pipeline, a small layer that lets a component reuse the numbers a shared tok2vec or transformer step computed once, instead of computing its own.
The text file (config.cfg) that fully describes a spaCy pipeline: its components, model designs and training settings, so a result can be reproduced exactly.
In spaCy, a named catalogue of functions (model designs, data readers, loggers and so on) that a config can refer to by name.
spaCy's compact format for storing many Docs together, used for training data and for moving results between programs.
spaCy's table that turns every string into a fixed number (its hash) and back, so each string is stored only once.
spaCy's entry for a word on its own, outside any sentence, holding facts that never change, such as whether it is a stop word.
Of the items a system labelled as X, the share that really are X. High precision means few false alarms.
Of the items that really are X, the share the system found. High recall means few misses.
One number that combines precision and recall; it stays low if either of them is low.

concepts.name: Installing spaCy and loading pipelines
concepts.summary: Install spaCy, download a trained pipeline package, and load it with spacy.load, or start empty with spacy.blank.
concepts.why: Nothing happens to your text without a pipeline, and the one you pick sets your accuracy, speed and memory use.
concepts.body:
**Natural language processing** (NLP) means getting computers to work with human language: splitting text into words, finding the names of people and places, working out how a sentence is built. **spaCy** is a fast Python library for NLP, used in real products as well as research.

spaCy is installed with `pip install spacy`, but the library alone knows very little about any language. That knowledge comes as a separate download, a trained **pipeline**: a series of processing steps plus the **machine learning models** they use, which are files of patterns learned from lots of example text. Install one with:

```bash
python -m spacy download en_core_web_sm
```

The name follows the scheme `language_type_genre_size`: `en_core_web_sm` is English, general-purpose ("core"), learned from web text, small. Sizes trade accuracy against speed and memory:
- `sm`: small and fast
- `md`, `lg`: bigger downloads that add **word vectors**, lists of numbers describing what each word means (used for similarity in a later lesson)
- `trf`: the most accurate and much slower, best run on a **GPU**, a graphics chip that speeds up this kind of maths (an Advanced lesson covers it)

`nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")` returns the pipeline as an object, by convention named `nlp`. Calling it on text, `nlp("Some text")`, runs every step on that text.

`spacy.blank("en")` creates a pipeline with only the language's basic rules for splitting text into words, and nothing learned. It's fast, and handy when rules are all you need, or as a starting point for teaching spaCy with your own examples later.

Pipeline packages are tied to a spaCy version: a pipeline for 3.8 expects spaCy 3.8.x. `python -m spacy validate` checks that your installed pipelines fit your spaCy. If your code will run on other computers, write the exact versions of both into `requirements.txt` so every machine gets the same ones. `nlp.meta` shows the pipeline's name, version and accuracy figures.
concepts.code:
import spacy

nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")     # after: python -m spacy download en_core_web_sm
print(nlp.meta["name"], nlp.meta["version"])   # core_web_sm 3.8.0
print(nlp.pipe_names)                  # the steps that run, in order
# ['tok2vec', 'tagger', 'parser', 'attribute_ruler', 'lemmatizer', 'ner']

doc = nlp("Apple is looking at buying a U.K. startup.")
print([t.text for t in doc])
# ['Apple', 'is', 'looking', 'at', 'buying', 'a', 'U.K.', 'startup', '.']

blank = spacy.blank("en")              # word-splitting rules only, nothing learned
print(blank.pipe_names)                # []
print(len(blank("Fast splitting only.")))   # 4

try:
    spacy.load("en_core_web_xx")
except OSError as e:
    print("OSError:", "E050" in str(e))  # True: package not installed
takeaways: Trained pipelines are separate downloads: python -m spacy download <name>
Names encode language, type, genre and size (sm, md, lg, trf)
spacy.load returns the nlp object; spacy.blank gives a rules-only pipeline
Keep pipeline and spaCy versions matched (check with `spacy validate`)
pitfalls: Expecting `pip install spacy` alone to make spacy.load('en_core_web_sm') work.

quiz.q: You need the most accurate results and have a GPU; speed is secondary. Which English pipeline fits best?
quiz.explain: The trf pipeline is the most accurate and runs much faster on a GPU.

quiz.q: What does `spacy.blank('en')` give you?
options: An error until you download a model
A pipeline with the language's basic rules but nothing learned
quiz.explain: A blank pipeline has only word-splitting rules and language data.

concepts.name: Doc, Token and Span
concepts.summary: Meet the three objects that hold every spaCy result, and see how spaCy keeps the original text intact.
concepts.why: Every spaCy result lives on these three objects, so moving around them easily is the core skill.
concepts.body:
Before a program can study words, it must split text into pieces. That is called **tokenization**, and each piece (a word, a number or a punctuation mark) is a **token**.

Calling `nlp(text)` splits the text into tokens, runs the rest of the pipeline, and returns a **`Doc`** holding the tokens plus everything the pipeline worked out about them. Three objects matter:
- `Doc`: the whole text. `len(doc)` counts tokens; loop over it or index it like a list.
- `Token`: `doc[i]`, one token, with `token.text`, `token.i` (its position in the doc), `token.idx` (the character position where it starts) and `token.whitespace_` (the space after it, if any).
- **`Span`**: `doc[start:end]`, a slice of several tokens, with `.text`, `.start`, `.end`, `.start_char` and `.end_char`. Sentences, names and search matches all come back as spans.

spaCy's tokenization is **non-destructive**: each token remembers the space after it, so `doc.text` gives back the input exactly, and `token.idx` lets you map results back to character positions, for example to highlight them.

The tokenizer first splits at spaces, then applies each language's rules for punctuation and special cases. That's why "U.K." stays one token while "don't" becomes "do" and "n't".

Tokens and spans don't hold their own copy of the data; they point into the Doc. Keep the Doc around while you use them. If you need to save a position for later, store `token.i` or character positions rather than the objects.

To get a span from character positions, for example ones another tool gave you, use `doc.char_span(start, end)`. It returns `None` if the positions fall inside a token; `alignment_mode="expand"` widens the span to the whole tokens around them.
concepts.code:
import spacy

nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")
doc = nlp("Don't ship it.  Test it first!")

print(len(doc), [t.text for t in doc])
# 10 ['Do', "n't", 'ship', 'it', '.', ' ', 'Test', 'it', 'first', '!']
tok = doc[2]
print(tok.text, tok.i, tok.idx, repr(tok.whitespace_))   # ship 2 6 ' '
print(doc.text == "".join(t.text_with_ws for t in doc))  # True: non-destructive

span = doc[6:9]
print(span.text, span.start, span.end, span.start_char)  # Test it first 6 9 16

print(doc.char_span(16, 23))                             # Test it
print(doc.char_span(17, 23))                             # None: not a token boundary
print(doc.char_span(17, 23, alignment_mode="expand"))    # Test it
takeaways: nlp(text) returns a Doc; doc[i] is a Token; doc[a:b] is a Span
Tokens keep the space after them, so the original text is recoverable
token.i is the token's position, token.idx its character position
doc.char_span maps character positions to a Span (or None)
pitfalls: Keeping Token or Span objects long after the Doc is gone; store positions instead.

quiz.q: Why does `doc.text` always equal the original input string?
options: spaCy stores a copy of the input separately
Each token records its trailing whitespace, making tokenization non-destructive
quiz.explain: Joining text_with_ws (the text plus its trailing space) of every token rebuilds the exact original.

quiz.q: What type is `doc[3:7]`?
quiz.explain: Slicing a Doc returns a Span view over those tokens.

concepts.name: Token attributes: lemma, POS, stop words
concepts.summary: Read lemma_, pos_, tag_, is_stop, like_num, shape_ and more, and know why each comes in a text form and a number form.
concepts.why: Most text clean-up is filtering or transforming tokens by these values.
concepts.body:
Each token carries **attributes**: named values attached to it, read with a dot like `token.text`. Some come from fixed language data; others are predictions made by the pipeline's models.

- `lemma_`: the **lemma**, the dictionary form you would look up ("running" becomes "run")
- `pos_`: the **part-of-speech tag**, the word type such as `NOUN`, `VERB`, `ADJ` or `PROPN` (a name); `tag_`: a more detailed tag (`VBG` means the -ing form of a verb in English)
- `morph`: grammar details such as `Tense=Past|VerbForm=Fin`

- `is_stop`: whether it is a **stop word**, a very common word like "the" or "of"
- `is_punct`, `is_alpha`, `is_digit`, `like_num`, `like_email`, `like_url`
- `shape_`: the pattern of its characters, like `Xxxxx` or `dd`; also `lower_`, `prefix_`, `suffix_`

The **trailing underscore** matters. `token.pos_` is the readable text; `token.pos` (no underscore) is a whole number that stands for it, a hash of the text. spaCy stores every string as such a number internally, because numbers are quicker to compare and take less memory. Use the underscore version unless you specifically need the numbers.

`spacy.explain("VBG")` describes a tag or label in plain English.

Flags like `is_stop` and `like_num` come from fixed language data and are always the same for a given word. `pos_`, `tag_` and `lemma_` are predictions (or look-ups based on them) and can be wrong on unusual text.

A typical clean-up is one comprehension: keep tokens that are alphabetic and not stop words, and take their lowercase lemmas. spaCy chooses each lemma using the predicted word type, so "saw" used as a verb becomes "see".
concepts.code:
import spacy

nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")
doc = nlp("The striped bats were hanging upside down, eating 12 mangoes.")

for t in doc[:5]:
    print(f"{t.text:8} {t.lemma_:6} {t.pos_:5} {t.tag_:4} {t.is_stop}")
# The      the    DET   DT   True
# striped  striped ADJ  JJ   False
# bats     bat    NOUN  NNS  False
# were     be     AUX   VBD  True
# hanging  hang   VERB  VBG  False

print(doc[9].text, doc[9].like_num, doc[9].shape_)    # 12 True dd
print(doc[4].morph)                                   # Aspect=Prog|Tense=Pres|VerbForm=Part
print(doc[2].pos, doc[2].pos_)                        # 92 NOUN  (id vs string)
print(spacy.explain("VBG"))                           # verb, gerund or present participle

clean = [t.lemma_.lower() for t in doc if t.is_alpha and not t.is_stop]
print(clean)   # ['striped', 'bat', 'hang', 'upside', 'eat', 'mango']
takeaways: lemma_, pos_, tag_ and morph are predictions by the pipeline
is_stop, is_alpha, like_num, shape_ come from fixed language data
Underscore = readable text; no underscore = a number (hash)
spacy.explain decodes tags and labels
pitfalls: Using `token.lemma` (a number) when you meant the text `token.lemma_`.

quiz.q: What is the difference between `token.pos_` and `token.tag_`?
options: pos_ is a broad word type, tag_ a more detailed tag
pos_ is the lemma, tag_ the entity label
tag_ is only set by spacy.blank
quiz.explain: pos_ uses broad types like VERB; tag_ uses detailed tags like VBG.

quiz.q: `print(token.lemma)` shows a large integer. Why?
options: Without the underscore you get the number (hash) that stands for the text
quiz.explain: spaCy stores strings as hashes; the underscore attribute returns the text.

concepts.name: Sentences and noun chunks
concepts.summary: Split text into sentences with doc.sents, pull out noun phrases with doc.noun_chunks, and choose a faster sentence splitter.
concepts.why: Sentences and noun phrases are natural units for summaries, search snippets and finding what a text is about.
concepts.body:
`doc.sents` gives one Span per sentence. In the trained English pipelines, sentence ends come from the **dependency parser**: the pipeline step that works out how the words of a sentence connect, such as which noun is the subject of which verb (a later lesson goes deeper). It's accurate, but it has to be switched on.

Each token also has `token.is_sent_start`, and `span.sent` gives the sentence a span belongs to.

If you only need sentences, there are faster options:
- the `sentencizer`, a step that splits on punctuation by rules: `nlp = spacy.blank("en"); nlp.add_pipe("sentencizer")`
- the learned `senter` step (included but switched off in the core pipelines), which is faster than the parser

`doc.sents` is a **generator**: it hands out sentences one at a time and can't be indexed. Wrap it in `list()` to index or count them. Asking for sentences when no step has set them raises an error (E030) telling you to add a parser, senter or sentencizer.

`doc.noun_chunks` gives **noun chunks**: a noun plus the words describing it, such as "Dr. Lee" or "the striped bats". They come from the dependency parse, so they need the parser, and they exist for languages with noun chunk rules (English, German, French and others). `chunk.root` is the main noun, and `chunk.root.head` the word the phrase hangs from, for example the verb it is the object of.

Noun chunks are a cheap way to find the main topics of a text, especially after dropping pronouns and counting the lemmas of their main nouns.
concepts.code:
import spacy

nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")
doc = nlp("Dr. Lee released a new dataset. The striped bats love ripe mangoes. Really!")

sents = list(doc.sents)
print(len(sents), [s.text for s in sents][:2])
# 3 ['Dr. Lee released a new dataset.', 'The striped bats love ripe mangoes.']

for chunk in doc.noun_chunks:
    print(f"{chunk.text:20} root={chunk.root.text:8} head={chunk.root.head.text}")
# Dr. Lee              root=Lee      head=released
# a new dataset        root=dataset  head=released
# The striped bats     root=bats     head=love
# ripe mangoes         root=mangoes  head=love

fast = spacy.blank("en")
fast.add_pipe("sentencizer")                 # rule-based, no model
print(len(list(fast("One. Two? Three!").sents)))   # 3
takeaways: doc.sents gives sentence Spans; in core pipelines the parser sets them
Use the sentencizer or senter when you need only sentences, faster
doc.noun_chunks gives noun phrases found by the parser
chunk.root and chunk.root.head link a phrase to its verb
pitfalls: Indexing doc.sents directly (doc.sents[0]); it's a generator, so use list(doc.sents).

quiz.q: Which component sets sentence boundaries in en_core_web_sm by default?
quiz.explain: Core English pipelines take sentence ends from the dependency parse.

concepts.name: Named entity recognition
concepts.summary: Extract people, organisations, places, dates and money with doc.ents, read labels, and set entities yourself.
concepts.why: Entities are what teams most often pull out of text: names, companies, amounts, dates and places.
concepts.body:
A named entity is a real-world thing with a name: a person, a company, a city, a date, an amount of money. Finding them is called **named entity recognition** (NER), and the pipeline's `ner` step does it with a trained model.

`doc.ents` is a tuple of `Span` objects, one per entity, each with `ent.text`, `ent.label_` (what kind of entity it is), `ent.start_char` and `ent.end_char`.

The English core pipelines use the OntoNotes labels, named after the collection of labelled text they learned from. They include:
- `PERSON`, `ORG`, `GPE` (countries, cities, states), `LOC` (other places, like mountains), `NORP` (nationalities, religious or political groups)
- `DATE`, `TIME`, `MONEY`, `PERCENT`, `QUANTITY`, `CARDINAL` (plain numbers), `ORDINAL` (first, second...)
- `PRODUCT`, `EVENT`, `WORK_OF_ART`, `LAW`, `LANGUAGE`, `FAC` (buildings, airports, roads)

`spacy.explain("NORP")` describes a label, and `nlp.get_pipe("ner").labels` lists every label the model knows.

On a single token, `token.ent_type_` gives the entity label and `token.ent_iob_` its **IOB** position: `B` for the first token of an entity, `I` inside one, `O` outside any entity.

Entities are predictions. Accuracy depends on the pipeline size and on how much your text resembles what the model learned from (news and web text). Lowercased text, or names from a narrow subject such as product codes or drug names, often needs extra rules (a later lesson) or teaching the model with your own examples.

You can replace the entities with `doc.ents = [...]`, using spans you make yourself, for example `Span(doc, start, end, label="PRODUCT")`, or use `doc.set_ents` for finer control. Entities can't overlap, because each token has only one entity tag; for overlapping spans use `doc.spans` groups instead. `displacy.render(doc, style="ent")` draws the text with its entities highlighted in colour.
concepts.code:
import spacy
from spacy.tokens import Span

nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")
doc = nlp("Apple paid $2 billion for a London startup on 5 May 2024, Tim Cook said.")

for ent in doc.ents:
    print(f"{ent.text:15} {ent.label_:6} {ent.start_char}-{ent.end_char}")
# Apple           ORG    0-5
# $2 billion      MONEY  11-21
# London          GPE    28-34
# 5 May 2024      DATE   46-56
# Tim Cook        PERSON 58-66

print(spacy.explain("GPE"))                  # Countries, cities, states
print(doc[0].ent_type_, doc[0].ent_iob_)     # ORG B
print(doc[1].ent_iob_)                       # O

doc.ents = list(doc.ents) + [Span(doc, 8, 9, label="PRODUCT")]   # "startup"
print([(e.text, e.label_) for e in doc.ents][2:4])
# [('London', 'GPE'), ('startup', 'PRODUCT')]
takeaways: doc.ents holds entity Spans with label_ and character positions
Core English labels follow OntoNotes: PERSON, ORG, GPE, DATE, MONEY...
token.ent_type_ and ent_iob_ show entities token by token
Set doc.ents yourself; use doc.spans for overlapping spans
pitfalls: Assuming the ready-made entity model knows drug names or product codes without extra rules or your own examples.

quiz.q: Which label does the English model use for 'France' in 'He moved to France'?
quiz.explain: Countries, cities and states are geo-political entities (GPE); LOC is for mountains, rivers and similar.

quiz.q: Why can't you put two overlapping spans into doc.ents?
options: Entities are stored as one IOB tag per token, so they can't overlap
Spans must be one token long
Only the NER step may set them
quiz.explain: Each token has one entity tag, so overlapping entities are impossible; use doc.spans instead.

concepts.name: Dependency parsing
concepts.summary: Walk the sentence tree with dep_, head, children and subtree to find who did what to whom.
concepts.why: Dependency links let you pull out subjects, objects and describing words, which a flat list of tokens or entities can't express.
concepts.body:
The dependency parser links every token to one other token, its **head**, with a label saying how they relate. The result is a tree: the main verb usually sits at the top (the root), and every other word hangs from it, directly or through other words.

- `token.dep_`: the relation to its head, such as `nsubj` (subject: who does it), `dobj` (direct object: what it's done to), `amod` (an adjective describing a noun), `prep`/`pobj` (a preposition and its object), `ROOT`
- `token.head`: the token it hangs from (the root is its own head)
- `token.children`, `token.lefts`, `token.rights`: the tokens hanging directly from it
- `token.subtree`: the token and everything below it, in order; `token.ancestors` walks upward

This structure answers questions that text patterns such as regular expressions can't. To find **who did what**, look for verbs and collect their `nsubj` and `dobj` children. To get the full phrase a word heads, take its subtree: `doc[t.left_edge.i : t.right_edge.i + 1]`, where `left_edge` and `right_edge` are the first and last tokens below it.

The English models use the ClearNLP label set (`spacy.explain` describes each label). Passive sentences ("the budget was approved by the manager") use `nsubjpass` and `agent`, so handle both forms when extracting relations.

`displacy.render(doc, style="dep")` draws the tree as a picture, and `displacy.serve(doc, style="dep")` shows it in your web browser. Looking at real parses is the fastest way to write correct extraction rules.

Parses are predictions and get worse on long, chatty or ungrammatical text. Write extraction rules defensively and test them on real data. The `DependencyMatcher` lets you describe tree patterns as data instead of writing the walking code yourself.
concepts.code:
import spacy

nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")
doc = nlp("The new manager quickly approved the large budget.")

for t in doc:
    print(f"{t.text:9} {t.dep_:7} <- {t.head.text}")
# The       det     <- manager
# new       amod    <- manager
# manager   nsubj   <- approved
# quickly   advmod  <- approved
# approved  ROOT    <- approved
# ...       budget is dobj <- approved

def phrase(t):                      # the whole phrase headed by token t
    return t.doc[t.left_edge.i : t.right_edge.i + 1].text

def svo(doc):                       # (subject, verb, object) triples
    found = []
    for verb in doc:
        if verb.pos_ != "VERB":
            continue
        subj = [c for c in verb.children if c.dep_ in ("nsubj", "nsubjpass")]
        obj = [c for c in verb.children if c.dep_ in ("dobj", "attr")]
        if subj and obj:
            found.append((phrase(subj[0]), verb.lemma_, phrase(obj[0])))
    return found

print(svo(doc))   # [('The new manager', 'approve', 'the large budget')]
takeaways: Every token has a head and a dep_ label; the root heads the sentence
children, subtree, left_edge and right_edge move around the tree
Combine the nsubj and dobj children of verbs to extract who did what
Draw parses with displacy before writing rules
pitfalls: Extracting only nsubj and missing passive sentences, which use nsubjpass.

quiz.q: In 'The dog chased the cat', what is the head of 'cat'?
quiz.explain: 'cat' is the direct object (dobj) of the verb 'chased'.

quiz.q: How do you get the whole phrase headed by a token t?
quiz.explain: left_edge and right_edge are the first and last tokens under t, so the slice is the full phrase.

concepts.name: Rule-based matching: Matcher and PhraseMatcher
concepts.summary: Find token patterns with the Matcher using attributes and operators, and long term lists with the PhraseMatcher.
concepts.why: Rules give precise, explainable results for things models miss, and are often all you need.
concepts.body:
The **`Matcher`** finds runs of tokens that fit a **pattern**: a list of dicts, one dict per token, each saying which attribute values that token must have.

```python
[{"LOWER": "machine"}, {"LOWER": "learning"}]
[{"POS": "ADJ", "OP": "*"}, {"POS": "NOUN"}]
[{"LIKE_NUM": True}, {"LOWER": {"IN": ["kg", "g"]}}]
```

Attributes include `TEXT`, `LOWER`, `LEMMA`, `POS`, `TAG`, `DEP`, `ENT_TYPE`, `IS_PUNCT`, `LIKE_NUM`, `SHAPE` and `LENGTH`. A value can be exact, or use `IN`, `NOT_IN`, `REGEX` (a regular expression, a mini-language for text patterns) or comparisons such as `{">=": 3}`. `"OP"` says how many times a token may appear: `?` optional, `*` zero or more, `+` one or more, `!` must not appear, `{n,m}` between n and m times.

Create it with `matcher = Matcher(nlp.vocab)` (the vocab is the pipeline's shared store of words), add patterns with `matcher.add("LABEL", [pattern1, pattern2])`, then call `matcher(doc)`. It returns `(match_id, start, end)` tuples, and `nlp.vocab.strings[match_id]` turns the id back into your label. With `OP`, matches can overlap; `greedy="LONGEST"` when adding, or `spacy.util.filter_spans`, keeps only the longest.

The **`PhraseMatcher`** is built for long lists of terms, such as a product catalogue or a list of place names. Its patterns are Docs: `matcher.add("DRUG", [nlp.make_doc(t) for t in terms])`. It stays fast with hundreds of thousands of terms. Pass `attr="LOWER"` to ignore capital letters.

Patterns that use `POS`, `LEMMA` or `DEP` need the trained steps that set them; `LOWER` and `TEXT` work even with `spacy.blank`. `as_spans=True` returns Span objects directly.
concepts.code:
import spacy
from spacy.matcher import Matcher, PhraseMatcher

nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")
doc = nlp("Order 3 kg of Green Tea and 250 g of green tea leaves. Ship 2 boxes.")

matcher = Matcher(nlp.vocab)
matcher.add("WEIGHT", [[{"LIKE_NUM": True}, {"LOWER": {"IN": ["kg", "g"]}}]])
matcher.add("ADJ_NOUN", [[{"POS": "ADJ", "OP": "+"}, {"POS": "NOUN"}]], greedy="LONGEST")
for match_id, start, end in matcher(doc):
    print(nlp.vocab.strings[match_id], doc[start:end].text)
# WEIGHT 3 kg
# WEIGHT 250 g
# ADJ_NOUN green tea   (relies on the tagger's POS predictions)

terms = ["green tea", "black tea", "oolong"]
pm = PhraseMatcher(nlp.vocab, attr="LOWER")         # case-insensitive
pm.add("TEA", [nlp.make_doc(t) for t in terms])
print([s.text for s in pm(doc, as_spans=True)])
# ['Green Tea', 'green tea']
takeaways: Matcher patterns are lists of per-token attribute dicts
OP (?, *, +, !) and IN, REGEX or comparisons add flexibility
PhraseMatcher matches long term lists fast; attr='LOWER' ignores case
Use greedy='LONGEST' or filter_spans to drop overlapping matches
pitfalls: Writing POS- or LEMMA-based patterns and running them with spacy.blank, where those attributes are empty.

quiz.q: Which pattern matches 'very big' and 'big' before 'house' (tagged ADV ADJ NOUN / ADJ NOUN)?
quiz.explain: The optional ADV token makes the pattern match with or without 'very'.

quiz.q: You need to tag 200,000 product names in text. Which tool fits?
quiz.explain: PhraseMatcher is designed for very long lists of exact terms.

concepts.name: EntityRuler and span rulers
concepts.summary: Add rule-based entities to the pipeline with the entity_ruler, combine it with the trained entity model, and decide who wins on overlaps.
concepts.why: Rules plus a model is the standard way to recognise entities from your own subject that the ready-made model doesn't know.
concepts.body:
The **`entity_ruler`** is a pipeline step that turns patterns into entities in `doc.ents`. Each pattern is a dict with a `label` and either a phrase string or a token pattern like the Matcher's:

```python
{"label": "ORG", "pattern": "Acme Corp"}
{"label": "TICKET", "pattern": [{"TEXT": {"REGEX": "^[A-Z]{2,5}-\\d+$"}}]}
```

Add it with `ruler = nlp.add_pipe("entity_ruler", before="ner")` and `ruler.add_patterns(patterns)`. **Where you place it** decides who wins:
- `before="ner"`: rule entities are set first, and the trained `ner` step respects them and predicts around them. Use this when your rules are trustworthy.
- after `ner` (the default, at the end of the pipeline): rules only fill gaps, unless you set `config={"overwrite_ents": True}`.

An `id` key in a pattern sets `ent.ent_id_`, which lets several spellings (such as "NYC" and "New York City") point to one standard id. Phrase patterns are split into tokens first, so they only match text that splits the same way; check odd strings such as product codes with `nlp.make_doc`.

Patterns can be saved and loaded as a JSON Lines file (one JSON object per line) with `ruler.to_disk("patterns.jsonl")` and `ruler.from_disk(...)`, and they're saved with the whole pipeline by `nlp.to_disk`. Phrase patterns use the PhraseMatcher inside, so thousands of names stay fast; set `phrase_matcher_attr="LOWER"` in the config to ignore capital letters.

For overlapping or nested labels that shouldn't go into `doc.ents`, the **`span_ruler`** writes to `doc.spans["ruler"]` instead.
concepts.code:
import spacy

nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")
ruler = nlp.add_pipe("entity_ruler", before="ner",
                     config={"phrase_matcher_attr": "LOWER"})
ruler.add_patterns([
    {"label": "PRODUCT", "pattern": "widgetpro 3000", "id": "wp3000"},
    {"label": "PRODUCT", "pattern": "widget pro", "id": "wp3000"},
    {"label": "TICKET", "pattern": [{"TEXT": {"REGEX": r"^[A-Z]{2,5}-\d+$"}}]},
])
print(nlp.pipe_names[-2:])          # ['entity_ruler', 'ner']

doc = nlp("Sarah from Acme reported OPS-1432 about the WidgetPro 3000 and the Widget Pro.")
for e in doc.ents:
    print(f"{e.text:15} {e.label_:8} {e.ent_id_}")
# Sarah           PERSON
# Acme            GPE       (trained model: wrong here, add a rule!)
# OPS-1432        TICKET
# WidgetPro 3000  PRODUCT  wp3000
# Widget Pro      PRODUCT  wp3000
takeaways: entity_ruler adds pattern-based entities to doc.ents
Put it before 'ner' to let rules take priority; after it to fill gaps
Pattern ids map several spellings to one standard id
span_ruler writes overlapping spans to doc.spans
pitfalls: Adding the ruler after 'ner' and wondering why rule matches that overlap model entities are ignored.

quiz.q: Your rules for product names must always win over the trained entity model. Where do you add the entity_ruler?
quiz.explain: Entities set before the ner step are kept, and it predicts around them.

concepts.name: Pipelines: components and nlp.pipe
concepts.summary: Inspect and control pipeline components, switch off what you don't need, and run many texts fast with `nlp.pipe`.
concepts.why: Handling lots of text quickly is mostly about working in batches and running only the steps you use.
concepts.body:
Each step of a pipeline is a **component**. `nlp.pipe_names` lists the components that run, in order, on every `nlp(text)` call: the tokenizer first (not listed), then for example `tok2vec`, `tagger`, `parser`, `attribute_ruler`, `lemmatizer` and `ner`. `nlp.get_pipe("ner")` returns one component; `nlp.add_pipe`, `remove_pipe`, `replace_pipe` and `rename_pipe` change the pipeline.

Running components you don't need wastes time. Three ways to skip them:
- `spacy.load(name, exclude=["parser", "ner"])`: never loaded
- `spacy.load(name, disable=[...])`: loaded but switched off; switch back on with `nlp.enable_pipe`
- `with nlp.select_pipes(enable=["tagger"]):` switches them off for one block only

Watch what depends on what: the lemmatizer needs the word types set by the tagger and attribute ruler, sentence ends come from the parser, and components that reuse the shared `tok2vec` step's results need it switched on.

For many texts, don't loop over `nlp(text)`. **`nlp.pipe(texts, batch_size=...)`** takes the texts in groups (batches) and hands back Docs one at a time as they're ready, which is much faster, especially for big pipelines running on a GPU. Pass `as_tuples=True` with `(text, context)` pairs to carry ids or other extra data along.

`n_process=2` or more runs several copies of the pipeline at once, one per processor core. Each copy loads its own model, so it only pays off for large jobs.

If you only need tokens, `nlp.make_doc(text)` runs just the tokenizer. `nlp.analyze_pipes(pretty=True)` reports what each component sets and needs.
concepts.code:
import time
import spacy

nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm", exclude=["parser"])
print(nlp.pipe_names)      # ['tok2vec', 'tagger', 'attribute_ruler', 'lemmatizer', 'ner']

texts = [f"Order {i} was shipped to Berlin on Monday." for i in range(2000)]

t = time.perf_counter()
docs = [nlp(t_) for t_ in texts[:500]]
loop = time.perf_counter() - t

t = time.perf_counter()
docs = list(nlp.pipe(texts[:500], batch_size=256))
batched = time.perf_counter() - t
print(batched < loop)       # True: batching is faster

with nlp.select_pipes(enable=["tok2vec", "ner"]):   # only what NER needs
    ents = [d.ents for d in nlp.pipe(texts[:3])]
print(ents[0])              # (Order 0, Berlin, Monday)

records = [("Paris is lovely.", {"id": 1}), ("I met Ana Lopez.", {"id": 2})]
for doc, ctx in nlp.pipe(records, as_tuples=True):
    print(ctx["id"], [e.text for e in doc.ents])    # 1 ['Paris'] / 2 ['Ana Lopez']
takeaways: pipe_names shows the components run on each call
exclude, disable and select_pipes skip components you don't need
nlp.pipe batches many texts and is much faster than a loop
as_tuples carries extra data; n_process runs several copies for big jobs
pitfalls: Calling nlp(text) in a loop over millions of texts instead of nlp.pipe.

quiz.q: What is the difference between exclude and disable in spacy.load?
options: disable removes the component from disk
exclude is only for the tokenizer
excluded components are not loaded at all; disabled ones are loaded but don't run and can be switched back on
quiz.explain: exclude saves loading time and memory; disable keeps the option to switch it back on.

quiz.q: Why does nlp.pipe outperform calling nlp() per text?
options: It handles texts in batches, so the models work on many texts at once
quiz.explain: Batching spreads fixed costs over many texts and lets the models process many docs together.

concepts.name: Word vectors and similarity
concepts.summary: Use the word vectors in md and lg pipelines to compare tokens, spans and documents, and know their limits.
concepts.why: Word vector similarity gives a quick 'find similar texts', duplicate spotting and grouping, without teaching any model.
concepts.body:
A word vector is a list of numbers (here 300 of them) describing a word, learned so that words used in similar ways get similar numbers. The `md` and `lg` pipelines include them. `lg` stores several hundred thousand distinct vectors; `md` keeps only 20,000 that many words share, so its similarities are rough (even unrelated words can end up with the same vector).

`token.vector` returns the vector as a NumPy array (NumPy is Python's main library for grids of numbers). `token.has_vector` and `token.is_oov` (out of vocabulary) tell you whether a word has one, and `nlp.vocab.vectors.shape` shows the table size.

`Doc.vector` and `Span.vector` are the **average** of their token vectors. `.similarity(other)` compares two vectors by the angle between them (cosine similarity): 1 means they point the same way, around 0 means unrelated. It works on tokens, spans and docs.

Useful, but know the limits:
- Averaging blurs meaning. Word order is lost, and long docs drift towards a bland average: "The dog bit the man" and "The man bit the dog" score as identical.
- There is one vector per word, mixing its meanings ("bank" of a river and of money).
- Similar is not the same as synonymous: "good" and "bad", or "cat" and "dog", are close because they appear in similar sentences.
- The `sm` pipelines have no real word vectors; similarity there falls back to other internal numbers, with a warning, and is unreliable.

For serious meaning-based search, sentence-embedding models (from the `sentence-transformers` library or a transformer pipeline) work far better: they turn a whole sentence into one vector and take word order into account. spaCy's vectors remain handy for quick prototypes and for finding related words with `nlp.vocab.vectors.most_similar`.
concepts.code:
import numpy as np
import spacy

nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_lg")           # lg: full table of word vectors
print(nlp.vocab.vectors.shape[1])            # 300 dimensions

cat, dog, car = nlp("cat dog car")
print(cat.vector.shape, cat.has_vector)      # (300,) True
print(round(cat.similarity(dog), 2), round(cat.similarity(car), 2))
# cat-dog clearly higher than cat-car

a = nlp("The dog bit the man.")
b = nlp("The man bit the dog.")
print(round(a.similarity(b), 3))             # 1.0  word order ignored!

print(round(nlp("good").similarity(nlp("bad")), 2))   # high: related, not synonyms

keys, _, scores = nlp.vocab.vectors.most_similar(
    np.asarray([nlp.vocab["coffee"].vector]), n=4)
print([nlp.vocab.strings[k] for k in keys[0]])   # e.g. coffee-related words
takeaways: lg ships a full word vector table, md a reduced one, sm none
Doc and Span vectors average token vectors; similarity compares their angle
Averages ignore word order and mix word meanings
Use sentence-embedding models for serious meaning-based search
pitfalls: Computing similarity with en_core_web_sm and trusting the numbers.

quiz.q: Why do 'The dog bit the man' and 'The man bit the dog' get similarity 1.0?
options: Doc vectors are averages of the same word vectors, so word order is lost
quiz.explain: Both docs contain the same tokens, and averaging is order-independent.

concepts.name: Custom components and extension attributes
concepts.summary: Write your own pipeline components with @Language.component or factories, and attach custom data via ._ extensions.
concepts.why: Custom components package your own logic as part of the pipeline, so every Doc comes out with everything you need already worked out.
concepts.body:
A component is any function (or other callable object) that takes a Doc and returns a Doc. Register it with a decorator so spaCy can add it by name and save it with the pipeline:

```python
@Language.component("flag_urgent")
def flag_urgent(doc):
    doc._.urgent = any(t.lower_ in {"asap", "urgent"} for t in doc)
    return doc

nlp.add_pipe("flag_urgent", last=True)
```

For components with settings or stored data (a lookup table, a model), use **`@Language.factory("name", default_config={...})`** on a function that receives `nlp`, `name` and the setting values and returns the component. Settings can then be passed in `add_pipe(..., config={...})` or written in a training config (see the training lesson).

**Extension attributes** add your own attributes to `Doc`, `Token` and `Span` under `._`, kept apart from spaCy's built-in ones:
- **attribute**: `Doc.set_extension("urgent", default=False)`, a value you can set on each object
- **getter**: `Token.set_extension("is_color", getter=lambda t: t.lower_ in COLORS)`, computed each time it's read
- **method**: `Span.set_extension("count", method=lambda span, w: ...)`

Register extensions once, when your module is imported; `force=True` replaces an existing one, which is useful when re-running code in a notebook.

Components should only add information, give the same output for the same input, and avoid heavy work at import time. Place them relative to others with `before=`/`after=` and mind what they need: a component reading `ent_type_` must run after `ner`. Extension values live in `doc.user_data` and are saved with the Doc when you use `DocBin(store_user_data=True)`.
concepts.code:
import spacy
from spacy.language import Language
from spacy.tokens import Doc, Span
Doc.set_extension("urgent", default=False, force=True)
Span.set_extension("is_money_big", force=True,
                   getter=lambda s: s.label_ == "MONEY" and "million" in s.text)

@Language.component("flag_urgent")
def flag_urgent(doc):
    doc._.urgent = any(t.lower_ in {"asap", "urgent"} for t in doc)
    return doc

@Language.factory("keyword_tagger", default_config={"keywords": ["refund"]})
def make_keyword_tagger(nlp, name, keywords):
    kw = set(keywords)
    def tagger(doc):
        doc.user_data["keywords"] = [t.text for t in doc if t.lower_ in kw]
        return doc
    return tagger
nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")
nlp.add_pipe("flag_urgent", after="ner")
nlp.add_pipe("keyword_tagger", config={"keywords": ["refund", "invoice"]})
doc = nlp("URGENT: refund the $3 million invoice ASAP.")
print(doc._.urgent, doc.user_data["keywords"])          # True ['refund', 'invoice']
print([(e.text, e._.is_money_big) for e in doc.ents])   # [('$3 million', True), ('ASAP', False)]
takeaways: A component is a Doc -> Doc function registered with @Language.component
Use @Language.factory for components with settings or stored data
Extensions on Doc, Token and Span live under ._ (attribute, getter, method)
Mind component order and needs with before= and after=
pitfalls: Registering extensions inside the component function, which runs on every Doc; register once at import.

quiz.q: When should you use @Language.factory instead of @Language.component?
options: Only for components that modify tokens
When the component needs settings or stored data such as a lookup table
When the component runs before the tokenizer
quiz.explain: Factories receive nlp and setting values, and build a component from them.

quiz.q: Which extension type computes its value on each access?
quiz.explain: Getter extensions call the function whenever the attribute is read.

concepts.name: Customising the tokenizer
concepts.summary: Add special cases and change prefix, suffix and infix rules so text such as code, units or hashtags splits into the right tokens.
concepts.why: Bad token boundaries break every later step: matchers, tags and entities all work on tokens.
concepts.body:
spaCy's tokenizer first splits at spaces, then examines each piece in turn:
- **special cases** (exceptions): exact strings with a fixed split, like "don't" into "do" + "n't"
- **prefixes** split off the start (quotes, brackets, currency signs), **suffixes** off the end (punctuation, units like "km"), again and again
- **infixes** split inside the piece (hyphens between letters, "/" between words)
- `token_match` and `url_match` protect strings that must stay whole

Special cases are the simplest fix: `nlp.tokenizer.add_special_case("gimme", [{ORTH: "gim"}, {ORTH: "me"}])`. The pieces' `ORTH` (exact text) values must join back into the original string. Special cases are also how you keep a term together, such as "C++" or "e.g.".

Prefix, suffix and infix rules are regular expressions. To change them, start from the language's defaults and build (compile) a new combined pattern:

```python
infixes = [p for p in nlp.Defaults.infixes if "-" not in p]
nlp.tokenizer.infix_finditer = compile_infix_regex(infixes).finditer
```

`compile_prefix_regex` and `compile_suffix_regex` do the same for prefixes and suffixes. `nlp.tokenizer.explain(text)` shows which rule produced each token, which is invaluable when output surprises you.

Changing tokenization after a model was trained means its steps now see token boundaries they never learned from, which can hurt accuracy; ideally customise before training. Tokenizer settings are saved with `nlp.to_disk`, but a completely custom tokenizer you write yourself must be registered to be loadable.
concepts.code:
import spacy
from spacy.attrs import ORTH
from spacy.util import compile_infix_regex

nlp = spacy.blank("en")
print([t.text for t in nlp("We use C++ and state-of-the-art 5km runs, gimme!")])
# ['We', 'use', 'C++', 'and', 'state', '-', 'of', '-', 'the', '-', 'art', '5', 'km', 'runs', ',', 'gimme', '!']

nlp.tokenizer.add_special_case("gimme", [{ORTH: "gim"}, {ORTH: "me"}])

infixes = [p for p in nlp.Defaults.infixes if "-|–|—" not in p]   # keep hyphenated words
nlp.tokenizer.infix_finditer = compile_infix_regex(infixes).finditer

doc = nlp("We use C++ and state-of-the-art 5km runs, gimme!")
print([t.text for t in doc])
# [..., 'state-of-the-art', '5', 'km', 'runs', ',', 'gim', 'me', '!']

for rule, text in nlp.tokenizer.explain("(5km)"):
    print(rule, text)
# PREFIX (  /  TOKEN 5  /  SUFFIX km  /  SUFFIX )
takeaways: Tokenization = split at spaces + special cases + prefix/suffix/infix rules
add_special_case fixes specific strings; ORTH pieces must rebuild the text
Recompile Defaults.prefixes/suffixes/infixes to change the rules
tokenizer.explain shows which rule made each token
pitfalls: Changing the tokenization of a trained pipeline and expecting its models to stay as accurate.

quiz.q: Which tool tells you why the tokenizer split '(5km)' the way it did?
quiz.explain: tokenizer.explain lists the rule (PREFIX, SUFFIX, INFIX, SPECIAL...) behind each token.

concepts.name: Training pipelines with configs and DocBin
concepts.summary: Prepare labelled data as DocBin files, generate a config, then train and evaluate a pipeline with the spacy train command.
concepts.why: Teaching the entity or text-category steps with your own examples is how spaCy goes from generic to accurate on your subject.
concepts.body:
spaCy trains from a **config** file that describes the whole pipeline: its components, the design of each model, and the hyperparameters (settings that control how learning runs). Because everything is written down, every experiment can be repeated exactly.

**1. Data.** Training examples are Docs carrying the correct answers (entities, categories, tags), saved in spaCy's binary **`DocBin`** format: build Docs, add them to `DocBin()`, and `to_disk("train.spacy")`. `python -m spacy convert` turns CoNLL, IOB and JSON files into `.spacy` files. Keep a separate `dev.spacy` for checking results.

**2. Config.** `python -m spacy init config config.cfg --lang en --pipeline ner --optimize efficiency` writes a complete config. Its sections cover `[paths]`, `[nlp]` (language and components), `[components]` (each component's model design), `[training]` (how learning runs: batch sizes, when to stop) and `[initialize]`. Any value can be replaced from the terminal: `--paths.train train.spacy`. Use `--optimize accuracy` or `--gpu` for transformer-based configs.

**3. Train.** `python -m spacy train config.cfg --output ./out --paths.train train.spacy --paths.dev dev.spacy`. At each checkpoint it prints the loss (how wrong the model still is) and scores on the dev data, and it saves `model-best` and `model-last`.

**4. Evaluate and use.** `python -m spacy evaluate out/model-best dev.spacy` reports **precision** (how many found entities are right), **recall** (how many real entities were found) and their combined **F-score** per label; `spacy.load("out/model-best")` loads it.

`python -m spacy debug data config.cfg` catches data problems early: entity spans that don't line up with tokens, labels missing from the dev data, labels with far fewer examples than others. To improve an existing pipeline instead of starting from scratch, take ("source") its components in the config. A few hundred good examples per label is a reasonable start.
concepts.code:
import spacy
from spacy.tokens import DocBin

nlp = spacy.blank("en")
TRAIN = [
    ("Order a WidgetPro for Ana", [(8, 17, "PRODUCT"), (22, 25, "PERSON")]),
    ("The GizmoMax broke again", [(4, 12, "PRODUCT")]),
]
db = DocBin()
for text, spans in TRAIN:
    doc = nlp.make_doc(text)
    ents = [doc.char_span(s, e, label=l) for s, e, l in spans]
    assert None not in ents, "span not aligned to tokens"
    doc.ents = ents
    db.add(doc)
db.to_disk("train.spacy")
print(len(DocBin().from_disk("train.spacy")))   # 2

# Then, in a shell:
#   python -m spacy init config config.cfg --lang en --pipeline ner --optimize efficiency
#   python -m spacy debug data config.cfg --paths.train train.spacy --paths.dev dev.spacy
#   python -m spacy train config.cfg --output ./out \
#          --paths.train train.spacy --paths.dev dev.spacy
#   python -m spacy evaluate out/model-best dev.spacy
# nlp = spacy.load("out/model-best")
takeaways: Correct answers live on Docs saved in DocBin (.spacy) files
spacy init config generates a complete, repeatable config
spacy train saves model-best and model-last; spacy evaluate scores them
spacy debug data catches misaligned spans and label problems
pitfalls: Creating entity spans whose character offsets don't align with token boundaries: char_span returns None and the example is broken.

quiz.q: Which file format does spacy train expect for training data?
quiz.explain: Training data is Docs saved in DocBin format; spacy convert creates them from other formats.

quiz.q: After training, which directory should you usually load?
quiz.explain: model-best holds the version with the best score on the dev data.

concepts.name: Transformer and LLM pipelines
concepts.summary: Use transformer-based pipelines such as en_core_web_trf, train with spacy-transformers, and know where spacy-llm fits.
concepts.why: Transformers give top accuracy inside the same spaCy code, at a real cost in speed and hardware.
concepts.body:
A **transformer** is a kind of large neural network that reads a whole passage at once and weighs how each word relates to every other; it's the design behind modern AI language models. The `trf` pipelines replace the small `tok2vec` step with a transformer (RoBERTa-base for English) through the `spacy-transformers` package. Your code stays the same: `nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_trf")`, then `doc.ents`, `token.dep_` and so on, with clearly better accuracy on parsing and entities.

Costs to plan for:
- Much slower on an ordinary processor (CPU); a GPU helps a lot. Call `spacy.prefer_gpu()` (or `require_gpu()`) before loading, with a GPU-enabled install such as `pip install spacy[cuda12x]`.
- More memory. Use `nlp.pipe` with a moderate `batch_size`.
- A transformer reads only a limited stretch of text at once; spaCy splits long docs into overlapping pieces and joins the results.
- No word vectors: `similarity` isn't meaningful with these pipelines.

To **train** your own transformer pipeline, generate a config with `spacy init config ... --optimize accuracy --gpu`. The `[components.transformer]` section names any model from Hugging Face, the main public site for sharing models, for example `bert-base-multilingual-cased` or one made for your subject. Later components connect to it through a **listener** layer, so they all share one transformer run.

**`spacy-llm`** is a separate package that adds components powered by large language models (LLMs) such as GPT or Claude. Instead of providing labelled examples, you describe the task in a prompt, written instructions for the model. It's useful for prototypes and for drafting labels that people then correct. Cost, slowness and inconsistent output usually push live systems towards a trained model.
concepts.code:
import spacy

using_gpu = spacy.prefer_gpu()          # False on CPU-only machines
print("GPU:", using_gpu)

try:
    nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_trf")  # pip: spacy-transformers + the package
    print(nlp.pipe_names)
    # ['transformer', 'tagger', 'parser', 'attribute_ruler', 'lemmatizer', 'ner']
    texts = ["Ada Lovelace worked with Charles Babbage in London."] * 8
    for doc in nlp.pipe(texts, batch_size=4):
        pass
    print([(e.text, e.label_) for e in doc.ents])
    # [('Ada Lovelace', 'PERSON'), ('Charles Babbage', 'PERSON'), ('London', 'GPE')]
except OSError:
    print("install with: python -m spacy download en_core_web_trf")

# Training config for a transformer pipeline:
#   python -m spacy init config cfg.cfg --lang en --pipeline ner --optimize accuracy --gpu
# [components.transformer.model]
# name = "roberta-base"            <- any Hugging Face model name
takeaways: trf pipelines use a transformer with the same spaCy code
Expect slower CPU speed and more memory; prefer_gpu() helps
Later components share one transformer through listeners
spacy-llm adds prompt-based components for prototyping
pitfalls: Calling .similarity() with a trf pipeline, which has no word vectors.

quiz.q: You call spacy.prefer_gpu() after spacy.load('en_core_web_trf'). What happens?
options: It moves the loaded model to the GPU
The model stays on CPU because GPU allocation must be chosen before loading
quiz.explain: prefer_gpu chooses the device for models loaded afterwards, so call it before loading.

concepts.name: The config system, registries and architectures
concepts.summary: Read and extend spaCy's config: value references, registered functions, model designs and the tok2vec listener pattern.
concepts.why: Every trained pipeline is defined by its config, and your own functions or model designs plug in through registries.
concepts.body:
A spaCy pipeline is fully described by its config, written in the format of Thinc (the machine learning library spaCy is built on): a text file of `[sections]` with `key = value` lines. `nlp.config` shows it for any loaded pipeline, and it is saved as `config.cfg` with the model. Sections nest with dots, such as `[components.ner.model]`, and values are written like JSON.

Two features make it powerful:
- **Interpolation**: `${section.key}` refers to another value, so a setting like a width or a path is defined once.
- **Registered functions**: a block containing `@architectures = "spacy.Tok2Vec.v2"`, `@misc = ...` or `@readers = ...` is replaced, when the config is read, by the result of calling that registered function with the block's other keys as arguments.

Each kind of function lives in a **registry**, a named catalogue: `architectures` (model designs), `misc`, `readers`, `loggers`, `optimizers`, `schedules` and more. Register your own with a decorator such as `@spacy.registry.misc("name.v1")`, or `@spacy.registry.architectures(...)` for a custom Thinc model. Put a version in the name (`.v1`, `.v2`) so old configs keep working after you change code. For `spacy train`, pass `--code my_functions.py` so your registrations are imported first.

Reading the config of `en_core_web_sm` shows the listener pattern. The shared `tok2vec` step turns each token into numbers (an embedding) once, and the tagger and parser reuse them through `spacy.Tok2VecListener.v1`, while the NER has its own internal `Tok2Vec`. That's why disabling `tok2vec` breaks the tagger but not the NER, and why further training of a shared tok2vec for one task can change the others. Training configs can give components independent copies when they must not interfere.
concepts.code:
import spacy
from thinc.api import Config

@spacy.registry.misc("keyword_set.v1")
def keyword_set(words: list, lower: bool = True) -> set:
    return {w.lower() if lower else w for w in words}

cfg = Config().from_str('''
[settings]
batch = 128
size = ${settings.batch}

[keywords]
@misc = "keyword_set.v1"
words = ["Refund", "Invoice"]
''')
print(cfg["settings"]["size"])                           # 128  (interpolated)
print(sorted(spacy.registry.resolve(cfg)["keywords"]))   # ['invoice', 'refund']

nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")
comps = nlp.config["components"]
print(comps["tagger"]["model"]["tok2vec"]["@architectures"])   # spacy.Tok2VecListener.v1
print(comps["ner"]["model"]["tok2vec"]["@architectures"])      # spacy.Tok2Vec.v2 (own copy)
print(comps["ner"]["model"]["@architectures"])                 # spacy.TransitionBasedParser.v2
takeaways: The config fully defines a pipeline; nlp.config shows it
${section.key} reuses values; @registry blocks call registered functions
Register your own functions and model designs with versioned names; use --code in training
Listeners let components share one tok2vec; the NER in core pipelines has its own
pitfalls: Renaming or changing a registered function without bumping its version, breaking older configs that reference it.

quiz.q: In a config, what does a block with `@architectures = 'spacy.Tok2Vec.v2'` become when resolved?
options: The object returned by calling the registered function with the block's other values
quiz.explain: Resolution looks up the registered function and calls it with the block's arguments.

quiz.q: Why does disabling `tok2vec` in en_core_web_sm break the tagger but not the NER?
options: The tagger listens to the shared tok2vec, while the NER has its own internal Tok2Vec
quiz.explain: The config shows a Tok2VecListener in the tagger and a full Tok2Vec inside the NER model.

concepts.name: Vocab, StringStore and hashes
concepts.summary: Understand how spaCy turns strings into fixed-size hash numbers, what lives in the Vocab and Lexemes, and how this affects memory.
concepts.why: Hashes explain the number-versus-text attributes, memory shared between Docs, and why the vocab grows in programs that run for a long time.
concepts.body:
spaCy never stores the same string twice. The **`StringStore`** (`nlp.vocab.strings`) turns every string into a 64-bit hash, a large whole number, and back: `strings["coffee"]` gives the hash, `strings[hash]` the text. A hash is computed from the string alone, so the same word gets the same number in every program and pipeline, which lets data be exchanged as plain integers.

The **`Vocab`** holds the StringStore, the word vector table, grammar data and **Lexemes**. A `Lexeme` is the entry for a word on its own, outside any sentence, with flags like `is_stop`, `is_alpha`, `like_num`, `lower_` and `shape_` that are the same wherever the word appears. A Token points to its Lexeme for these attributes and adds the ones that depend on the sentence (tag, dependency, entity).

Docs store token data as compact fixed-size records of numbers (hashes, plus references to the shared entries), so they're memory-efficient. `doc.to_array([LOWER, POS, ENT_TYPE])` exports chosen attributes as a NumPy `uint64` array (a grid of whole numbers) in one call, and `doc.count_by(attr)` counts values quickly.

A consequence: to turn a hash back into text you need a StringStore that has seen the string. Docs rebuilt from bytes in another process need their strings sent along too, which `DocBin` handles.

In a program that runs for a long time, every new string (typos, ids, web addresses) is added to the StringStore and stays there, so memory slowly grows. Fix it by reloading the pipeline now and then, or by doing the work in worker processes that are replaced from time to time.
concepts.code:
import spacy
from spacy.attrs import IS_ALPHA, LOWER, POS

nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")
strings = nlp.vocab.strings

h = strings["coffee"]
print(h)                              # 3197928453018144401
print(strings[h])                     # coffee
print(spacy.blank("de").vocab.strings["coffee"] == h)   # True: same hash anywhere

doc = nlp("I love coffee and coffee loves me")
print(doc[2].orth == doc[4].orth == h)                  # True
lex = nlp.vocab["coffee"]
print(type(lex).__name__, lex.is_alpha, lex.shape_)    # Lexeme True xxxx

arr = doc.to_array([LOWER, POS, IS_ALPHA])
print(arr.shape, arr.dtype)           # (7, 3) uint64
counts = doc.count_by(LOWER)
print(counts[h])                      # 2

n = len(strings)
nlp("zxqv-unique-id-91")
print(len(strings) > n)               # True: new strings accumulate
takeaways: StringStore maps strings to fixed 64-bit hashes and back
Lexemes hold word facts that don't depend on the sentence; Tokens add the rest
doc.to_array and count_by export attributes efficiently
The StringStore grows with every new string in long-running programs
pitfalls: Sending hashes to another process and trying to decode them with a StringStore that never saw those strings.

quiz.q: Why is the hash of 'coffee' the same in two unrelated spaCy pipelines?
options: Both use the same model file
The hash is computed from the string itself
quiz.explain: The hash is a pure function of the string, so any StringStore produces the same id.

quiz.q: Which attribute is stored on the Lexeme rather than the Token?
quiz.explain: is_stop doesn't depend on context, so it lives on the shared Lexeme.

concepts.name: Serialization and scaling out
concepts.summary: Save pipelines and Docs efficiently, send Docs between processes with DocBin, and run spaCy on lots of text with several processes.
concepts.why: Real systems process millions of documents; storing results and running in parallel correctly matter as much as the model.
concepts.body:
**Pipelines**: `nlp.to_disk(path)` writes a folder with `config.cfg`, `meta.json`, the vocab, tokenizer settings and each component's learned weights; `spacy.load(path)` restores it. `spacy package` turns that folder into an installable Python package, convenient for installing on servers. Your custom components and factories must be imported before loading, or `spacy.load` fails with an unknown factory error.

**Docs**: avoid pickling single Docs. Each pickle includes vocab strings, so pickling many Docs is large and slow. `DocBin(attrs=[...], store_user_data=True)` stores many Docs compactly with one shared string table: `db.add(doc)`, then `db.to_bytes()` or `to_disk()`, and later `list(db.get_docs(nlp.vocab))`. With `store_user_data`, custom `._` values travel too.

Often you don't need the Doc at all: pull out what you need (entity tuples, lemmas, or JSON via `doc.to_json()`) inside the worker and return plain data. That is the cheapest thing to move between processes.

**Scaling**:
- `nlp.pipe(texts, n_process=4, batch_size=...)` uses several processes; each loads its own copy of the model, so memory use multiplies.
- Switch off components you don't need before starting the extra processes.
- Set the thread count of the underlying maths libraries to 1 per process, so the processes don't fight over the CPU cores.
- On a GPU, use a single process with a larger batch.
- To spread work over many machines, run the same function in Spark, Ray or Dask workers, loading `nlp` once per worker rather than once per task.
concepts.code:
import spacy
from spacy.tokens import DocBin, Doc

Doc.set_extension("source", default=None, force=True)
nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm", exclude=["parser"])

texts = ["Ada met Alan in London.", "Grace worked at Harvard.", "Paris in May."]
db = DocBin(store_user_data=True)
for i, doc in enumerate(nlp.pipe(texts)):
    doc._.source = f"doc-{i}"
    db.add(doc)
data = db.to_bytes()                          # compact, shared strings
print(len(data) < 10_000)                     # True

restored = list(DocBin().from_bytes(data).get_docs(nlp.vocab))
print(restored[1]._.source, [e.text for e in restored[1].ents])   # doc-1 ['Grace', 'Harvard']

def extract(texts):                           # return plain data, not Docs
    return [[(e.text, e.label_) for e in d.ents]
            for d in nlp.pipe(texts, n_process=2, batch_size=64)]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(extract(texts * 2)[0])              # [('Ada', 'PERSON'), ('Alan', 'PERSON'), ('London', 'GPE')]
    nlp.to_disk("my_pipeline")
    print(spacy.load("my_pipeline").pipe_names[-1])   # ner
takeaways: nlp.to_disk and spacy.load(path) save and restore whole pipelines
DocBin stores many Docs compactly with shared strings; avoid pickling Docs
Return plain extracted data from workers when you can
n_process multiplies model memory; on a GPU use one process with big batches
pitfalls: Loading the spaCy model inside the function that handles each item of a parallel job, reloading it thousands of times.

quiz.q: Why prefer DocBin over pickling a list of Docs?
options: DocBin stores the strings once for all Docs and only the chosen attributes, so it is much smaller and faster
quiz.explain: Pickled Docs each carry vocab data, while DocBin shares one string table.

quiz.q: A spacy.load of your saved pipeline fails with an unknown factory error. What is missing?
options: The module defining the custom component wasn't imported before loading
quiz.explain: Custom factories are registered at import time, so the code must be imported first.
